beliefs.practice: Never commit the connection string or secrets to source control: read the DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment at runtime and (in production) retrieve the connection string from a secrets store such as Azure Key Vault. Provide only a .env.example with a placeholder.

Create a single Motor (AsyncIOMotorClient) instance per process and reuse it across the app (do not create a new client per request). Configure connection pooling (e.g., maxPoolSize) and sensible timeouts (connectTimeoutMS, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) via the client URI or options.

Require TLS/SSL for connections (tls=true/ssl=true) and validate certificates (do not disable certificate validation). Use connection string parameters to enforce TLS and strong cipher suites where supported.

Use least-privilege database credentials: create a database user limited to the sample_fintech_14 database and grant only the roles required (read/write only on the collections used), avoid using admin/root credentials in the app.

Model each loan application as a single document with these fields at minimum: _id (ObjectId), application_id (unique string), state (enum), version (int), transitions (array of {from, to, actor, ts, note}), created_at, updated_at. Add a separate field for next_action_at if the orchestrator queries by schedule.

Make state transitions atomic with a single find_one_and_update (or equivalent atomic update): include the expected current state (or version) in the filter, use $set to change state and increment version, and $push to append a transition log entry in the same update so the transition and log are always in sync.

Implement optimistic concurrency control: include a version or expected state in update filters (e.g., {application_id: X, state: 'underwriting', version: N}) and treat a non-match as a conflict so the orchestrator retries or re-reads. Do not rely on last-write-wins for critical workflow steps.

Avoid unbounded growth of the transitions array in the application document (which can hit document size limits). Either cap the in-document array (max N entries) or store transition history in a separate transitions collection keyed by application_id.

Create a compound index to efficiently find work: at minimum index {state:1, next_action_at:1} (or {state:1, updated_at:1}) so the orchestrator can query pending applications cheaply. If you query by application_id, make that field unique with an index.

When using Beanie/ODM, declare indexes in the document model or call create_indexes on startup so the app's expected indexes are created programmatically (e.g., unique index on application_id and the compound indexes needed).

Use TTL indexes for ephemeral or time-bound documents (e.g., short-lived tasks, temp artifacts, or audit entries you want auto-pruned) by creating an index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds set.

For vector search, store a dense float vector field and create a platform-supported vector index (specifying dimension and metric). Provide explicit index parameters (index type e.g., hnsw/diskann/ivf, dimension, metric like cosine or innerProduct) and test retrieval performance on representative vectors.
Normalize and/or L2-normalize vectors if you intend to use cosine similarity; store vectors in a compact float32 representation where supported to minimize storage and speed index operations.

Use exponential backoff with jitter for retries on transient errors (network timeouts, 429/TooManyRequests), and make retries idempotent where possible. Limit total retry attempts to avoid cascading load spikes.

Monitor and tune throughput: observe RU/s (or the Mongo-compatible throughput metrics provided) and provision autoscale or appropriate RU/s to avoid throttling. Record and alert on 429s and long-running ops.

Prefer single-document atomic updates over multi-document transactions for orchestrator state changes; only use multi-document transactions when you genuinely need atomicity across multiple collections, since transactions add latency and throughput cost.

Avoid storing secrets or raw LLM system prompts in the database; store references or encrypted blobs instead. For sensitive PII in applications, use field-level encryption or separate encrypted storage.

Use change streams (or the cloud provider's change feed) or a logical work-queue pattern instead of naive polling when possible: drive the orchestrator from change notifications to lower cost and latency.
Keep documents small and project only required fields in queries (use .find({}, projection)) to reduce RU cost and network transfer when listing pending applications or fetching large histories.

Cap the size of individual documents to avoid MongoDB / cluster document size limits (16MB): if transition history or attachments can grow unbounded, move them to separate collections or object storage and reference them.

Use explain() to validate that queries hit the intended index; test representative queries (orchestrator worker queries, agent lookups, vector nearest-neighbor) and adjust indexes before rolling to production.
Restrict network access to the cluster with firewall rules, VNet/private endpoint or IP restrictions; do not expose the database publicly without network controls.

Implement schema versioning in documents (a schema_version field) and write idempotent, backward-compatible migration scripts that run as a controlled deployment step rather than inline during reads/writes.

When using Beanie + Motor, ensure the client is created with consistent UUID/ObjectId handling (e.g., set uuidRepresentation if required) and call init_beanie(database=...) at app startup to register document models and create indexes if desired.

Consider client-side field-level encryption for particularly sensitive fields (SSNs, bank account numbers) if regulatory requirements demand it; otherwise rely on platform-managed at-rest encryption and transport-layer TLS.
